San Diego and Imperial Counties: California Science Test (CAST) School Landscape

Which schools in the UC San Diego Science Project region are beating the odds in science, which face the largest gaps, and what we can learn from both.

UC San Diego Science Project (UC San Diego CREATE)  |  Last updated: October 19, 2026  |  Version 1.3

Overview

The UC San Diego Science Project is one of the regional sites of the California Science Project, serving the K-12 science teachers and districts of San Diego and Imperial Counties through professional learning and research-practice partnerships. We built this dashboard to ground that work in evidence, and we share it with district partners, the San Diego County Office of Education, and colleagues across the California Science Project network who may want to repeat the analysis for their own regions (every source is public and the build is documented under Methods).

The dashboard maps California Science Test (CAST) results for every public school in San Diego and Imperial Counties across the test's seven administrations (2018-19 through 2025-26), and asks one question of each school: how does it perform compared with California schools serving similar students? Schools that land well above that comparison line are beating the odds; schools well below it face the largest gaps. Both are places a science project can learn from and partner with.

Scope: CAST is given once in elementary school (grade 5), once in middle school (grade 8), and once in high school (in grade 10, 11, or 12, at the school's choice), so results are analyzed in three grade spans. Throughout, "SED" means socioeconomically disadvantaged (the state's definition, which includes students eligible for free or reduced-price meals), "EL" means English learner, and "URG" means the share of students from groups underrepresented in STEM (Hispanic or Latino, Black, American Indian, Pacific Islander). Every school with at least 11 tested students in a year is included, including charter, county office, and alternative programs; alternative programs are shown in their own section of the rankings rather than ranked against comprehensive schools.

Headline findings

    How to use this dashboard

    • Reading the Model explains, in plain language, what "predicted" and "residual" mean. Start there if the idea of a demographic baseline is new.
    • Explore Schools is the interactive scatterplot: pick a grade span and year, choose what goes on each axis (percent socioeconomically disadvantaged, percent eligible for free or reduced-price meals, percent English learners, or percent of students from groups underrepresented in STEM, plotted against percent met or exceeded or mean scale score), hover for names, click a dot to pin a school and see its seven-year trend.
    • School Trends answers who is rising and who is falling: search any school for its full 2018-19 to 2025-26 history, see the largest sustained gains and declines since 2023, and compare county and district trajectories.
    • Beating the Odds lists consistent overperformers and the largest gaps among high-need schools, with the need threshold under your control.
    • District Patterns shows where a district's schools cluster above or below the line, described, never diagnosed.

    Read every number with these limits in mind

    CAST is one assessment on one day. A residual of a few points is noise; a residual of 10 or more points sustained across four or five years is a signal. The model describes the statewide average relationship between demographics and scores; it never says what any student can achieve. Participation varies by school and year and dips at high schools that test in grade 12. 2020-21 had very low participation and is shown but never used for rankings. Full caveats are in Methods and Limitations.

    Reading the Model

    The analysis rests on one idea, borrowed from decades of school-effectiveness research: to judge a school fairly, compare it with schools serving similar students, not with every school in the state.

    Step 1: the data

    Scores come from the CAST research file, a public data table that CDE's testing contractor (ETS) posts each October after the spring administration. It is not student-level data: for every school, every grade tested, and every student group, it reports how many students were enrolled, tested, and scored, the mean scale score, and the percent at each achievement level. The student-group breakdowns come from the enrollment records districts submit to CALPADS, which ETS joins to each student's test result before aggregating. Any row with fewer than 11 students is blank for privacy. One statewide file per year holds every school in California; the dashboard uses the school-level All Students rows for grade 5, grade 8, and the combined high school grades.

    Demographics come from a second CDE file, the Dashboard Census Enrollment file, which reports for every school the percent of its Census Day enrollment (the first Wednesday of October, the same CALPADS submission) in each student group. "Socioeconomically disadvantaged" is the state's definition: eligible for free or reduced-price meals, or neither parent completed high school, or homeless, foster, or migrant. The two files are joined on each school's 14-digit county-district-school code, giving one row per school per year with its score and its demographics for the same school year. Percent FRPM is added from CDE's student poverty file in the same way.

    Step 2: the statewide line (what the dashed line on the scatterplot is)

    The dashed line is purely descriptive, one variable at a time. For grade 5 in 2025-26, for example, start with all 5,792 California elementary schools with at least 11 fifth graders tested. For the point drawn at 72.5 percent SED, keep the schools whose SED is between 70.0 and 74.9 percent (there are 352), take each school's percent met or exceeded, and average those 352 numbers with each school counting once. That mean (28.5 percent) is the height of the point. Repeat for every 5-point band from 0 to 100 and connect the points; a band is drawn only if it holds at least 15 schools. The Explore tab lets you switch the line between the mean and the median of each band.

    The dashed line answers "what does a typical California school at this level of one variable score?" It cannot answer "what about a school at 72 percent SED and 60 percent English learners?", because the 352 schools in that band range from 0.5 to 69 percent EL. That is what the model is for.

    Step 3: the model (where "predicted" comes from)

    For each span and year, all California schools in the pool are fit at once with ordinary least squares regression, the same method as a spreadsheet trendline but with several variables together:

    predicted % met = b0 + b1·SED + b2·(SED²/100) + b3·EL + b4·Hispanic/Latino + b5·Black + b6·American Indian + b7·Pacific Islander + b8·SWD + b9·ln(students tested)

    Each variable is a percent of the school's enrollment (students tested is a count). "Least squares" means the ten b values are chosen to make the sum, over all schools in the pool, of (actual minus predicted)² as small as possible. There is exactly one answer; no judgment enters beyond the choice of variables. The SED² term lets the line bend, since the drop from 0 to 20 percent SED is steeper than the drop from 80 to 100. A school missing a demographic value (under 1 percent of schools) gets the statewide median for that variable. The same regression is run a second time with mean scale score as the outcome.

    Plug any school's own percentages into the equation and you have its predicted score: what a typical California school with that exact profile scored that year. The residual is actual minus predicted. The dashed line and the prediction usually agree closely, but they differ for schools whose other characteristics are far from average for their SED level, and the residual always uses the prediction, never the dashed line.

    Worked example

    Pick any school in the region to see every term of the equation filled in for a given year. The default is a school whose prediction differs noticeably from the dashed line because of its English learner share.

    What the model is not

    • It is not a prediction about any individual student, and it does not lower expectations for anyone. It sets the comparison bar where a school actually stands, so that a school at 90 percent SED scoring 33 percent met is recognized as the standout it is.
    • It does not explain why a residual is positive or negative. Curriculum, time for science, teacher preparation, assessment conditions, and participation are all invisible to it. Residuals point to where to look; conversations with the school explain what is there.
    • It is linear, so it is least reliable at the extremes (very small schools, continuation and alternative programs where predictions can approach zero). Those schools are kept in the dataset but reported separately.

    Explore Schools

    Each dot is one school in one year. Hover for the school; click to pin it and see its history.

    Two different reference lines, read them differently

    The dashed line is the statewide average (or median, your choice) score of California schools in each 5-point band of whatever single variable is on the x-axis. It is descriptive and accounts for that one variable only. The residual in the tooltip and tables comes from the multi-variable model (see Reading the Model), which accounts for SED, English learners, ethnicity, students with disabilities, and school size together. A dot can sit above the dashed line and still carry a small or negative residual if, for example, its English learner share is far below other schools at its SED level. To see residuals exactly, set the x-axis to Model prediction: the solid 45-degree line is the model, and each dot's vertical distance from it is its residual.

    School Trends

    Who is gaining ground, who is losing it, and who has held strong. Trends are measured on the residual (the school's distance from demographically similar California schools), not on raw percent met, because raw scores rose statewide every year since 2022 and nearly every school "improved" in raw terms. A rising residual means the school improved faster than the state; a falling one means it fell behind the state's pace. Raw scores are shown alongside so nothing is hidden.

    Making sense of the pandemic years

    Headline trends use 2023 through 2026 (four administrations). 2022 was the first full-participation year after the pandemic and many schools were still recovering, so it is drawn in the charts but excluded from the trend slope. 2020-21 had roughly 15 percent participation statewide and is drawn faint and marked with an asterisk. 2018-19 predates both the pandemic and the revised CAST blueprint introduced in 2021-22, so it is a useful anchor but not strictly comparable. There was no test in 2019-20.

    Movers, 2023 to 2026

    Trend is the least-squares slope of the residual across the four administrations, in points per year. Rising means a slope of +2.5 or more per year with the 2026 residual above 2023; falling is the mirror; everything else is stable. Lists are limited to comprehensive schools with all four years and at least 30 tested students on average, so that a few students cannot produce a trend. Alternative programs and smaller schools are still searchable above.

    Beating the Odds

    Schools are summarized over the five full administrations since the pandemic (2022 through 2026) and must have at least three years of data. Consistent overperformers average at least 5 points above their predicted score and were above prediction in all but at most one year. Largest gaps average at least 5 points below and were below in all but at most one year. Both lists are restricted to high-need schools by the threshold you set.

    District Patterns

    When most of a district's schools land on the same side of the line, year after year, the pattern is more likely to reflect something district-wide (curriculum, instructional minutes for science, assessment conditions, professional learning) than anything about one school. This tab reports those patterns and nothing more: where they occur, how large they are, and how consistent. It does not say why.

    Only comprehensive schools (alternative programs excluded) and only districts with at least three schools in the span are shown. "Share of school-years above" is the percent of that district's school-year observations with a positive residual; 50 percent is what chance would produce.

    What stands out

    Pairing with district plans

    The UC San Diego Science Project maintains a companion dashboard that reads every district's Local Control and Accountability Plan (LCAP) in the region and records what each plans and budgets for science professional learning and who staffs science support. Where a district appears at either end of the tables above, that LCAP record is the natural next thing to read. One verified example: Cajon Valley Union's 2025-26 LCAP (Goal 2, Action 2.12) states that a team of instructional coaches was provided but "no science coach was hired" because of shifts in induction needs, and its NGSS implementation self-reflection score fell from 3.01 to 2.74 (LCAP PDF). That is a documented fact from the district's own plan, placed beside the data; whether the two are related is a question for a conversation, not a conclusion of this analysis.

    High School Grade Tested

    High schools choose whether to give CAST in grade 10, 11, or 12 (or a mix). The research files report each tested grade separately, so the pattern is observable. A school is labeled by a grade when 70 percent or more of its tested students were in that grade; otherwise it is "mixed."

    Imperial County

    Imperial County, east of San Diego along the Mexican border, is the rural half of the region: 16 districts serving about 37,000 students, with a student population that is about 94 percent Hispanic or Latino and 40 percent English learners, with 80 percent or more of students socioeconomically disadvantaged at most schools. Against that profile, the county's science results are not uniformly behind the state line, and the variation among its schools is the most useful thing in this tab.

    Methods and Limitations

    Data assembly

    • CAST results: the statewide "All Student Groups" research file for each administration (2018-19, 2020-21, 2021-22, 2022-23, 2023-24, 2024-25, 2025-26), downloaded from the CAASPP reporting site. School-level rows for the All Students group and for socioeconomically disadvantaged, English learner, Hispanic or Latino, and Black or African American students were kept, at grades 5, 8, 10, 11, 12, and the combined high school aggregate. Cells with fewer than 11 students are suppressed in the source and appear as blank. Three file layouts (2019; 2021-2023; 2024-2026) were reconciled by column name. 2025-26 relabeled achievement levels (Minimal, Developing, Proficient, Advanced); "Proficient and Above" is treated as the continuation of "Met and Above." The 2018-19 file has no combined high school row, so one was built from the grade 10, 11, and 12 rows weighted by students with scores.
    • Demographics: the California School Dashboard Census Enrollment files for the matching academic year (percent SED, English learner, each race/ethnicity, students with disabilities, homeless, foster), and the CDE Unduplicated Student Poverty (FRPM) files, with percent FRPM computed from counts. Percent URG sums Hispanic or Latino, Black, American Indian or Alaska Native, and Native Hawaiian or Pacific Islander.
    • School attributes: the CDE Public Schools and Districts directory (school type, educational option, charter status, grade span, status, coordinates).
    • Alternative programs are flagged when the directory lists a non-traditional educational option (continuation, alternative school of choice, community day, juvenile court, county community, opportunity, special education, independent study), when the school is primarily or exclusively virtual, or when the name indicates a continuation, virtual, or home-study program.

    Model

    • For each span and year, ordinary least squares on all California schools with at least 11 tested students: outcome = percent met or exceeded (and separately, mean scale score); predictors = percent SED, SED squared (to allow curvature), percent EL, percent Hispanic or Latino, Black, American Indian, Pacific Islander, students with disabilities, and log of students tested. Missing predictors are set to the statewide median for that span-year (fewer than 1 percent of schools).
    • Residual = actual minus predicted. The z-score divides the residual by that span-year's residual standard deviation (about 10 to 12 points), so a z of 1.5 is roughly the top 7 percent statewide.
    • Multi-year summaries average residuals over 2022 through 2026 for schools with at least three of those years. 2018-19 and 2020-21 are available in Explore Schools but excluded from rankings: 2019 predates the pandemic and the revised CAST blueprint, and 2021 had very low participation.

    Limitations

    • One test, one day. CAST is a single annual measure of a subset of the NGSS. It does not capture science learning in grades other than those tested, nor engineering practices or lab work.
    • Residuals are not causes. A positive residual is consistent with strong science instruction, but also with selective enrollment (magnets, charters with application processes), with assessment conditions, or with small-sample luck. A negative residual is consistent with little science instruction, but also with low participation, testing in a less-prepared grade, or a cohort effect. The dashboard describes; it does not diagnose.
    • Small schools swing. With 11 to 30 tested students, a few students move the percentage several points. The multi-year averages and "years above" counts are the defense; treat single-year results for small schools as provisional.
    • High school participation. Tested divided by enrolled falls below 80 percent at many high schools, particularly those testing in grade 12. Lower participation can bias results in either direction.
    • Demographics are school-wide, not grade-specific. The Census Enrollment percentages describe the whole school; the tested grade may differ somewhat.
    • Charter and county-office codes change. A few schools changed CDS codes across years (notably some charters in 2019) and appear as separate records; their multi-year summaries may be shorter than their real history.
    • Linear fit at the extremes. Predictions for schools at 95 to 100 percent SED with very high EL can approach or fall below zero, especially at high school. Those schools' residuals are shown but should be read against their actual scores.

    Glossary

    CAST
    California Science Test, the state's NGSS-aligned science assessment, part of CAASPP. First operational in 2018-19; given in grades 5, 8, and once in high school.
    Percent met or exceeded
    Share of tested students at the top two of four achievement levels (Standard Met and Standard Exceeded; relabeled Proficient and Advanced in 2025-26).
    Mean scale score
    Average scale score of tested students; roughly 150 to 250 at grade 5, 350 to 450 at grade 8, 550 to 650 in high school. More sensitive than percent met at the low end of the range.
    SED
    Socioeconomically disadvantaged: eligible for free or reduced-price meals, or neither parent completed high school, or homeless, foster, or migrant. The state's standard poverty measure.
    FRPM
    Eligible for free or reduced-price meals under the National School Lunch Program; the measure most of the research literature uses. Nearly identical to SED for most schools.
    EL
    English learner, excluding students reclassified as fluent.
    URG
    Percent of students from groups underrepresented in STEM fields: Hispanic or Latino, Black or African American, American Indian or Alaska Native, Native Hawaiian or Pacific Islander.
    SWD
    Students with disabilities.
    Predicted
    What a typical California school with this school's demographic profile scored that year, from the model described under Reading the Model.
    Residual
    Actual minus predicted, in proficiency points. Positive means above demographically similar schools statewide.
    School-year
    One school observed in one test year. A district with 6 schools over 5 years has up to 30 school-years.
    Alternative program
    Continuation, community day, county community, juvenile court, opportunity, independent study, and primarily virtual schools, plus county office programs. Kept in the data, listed separately.
    LCAP
    Local Control and Accountability Plan, the three-year plan each California district adopts and updates annually to describe goals, actions, and spending.
    CDE, CAASPP, CALPADS
    California Department of Education; California Assessment of Student Performance and Progress (the state testing system); California Longitudinal Pupil Achievement Data System (the state's student data system).

    Refreshing this dashboard

    The dataset is embedded in this file as const DATA, so the single HTML file is self-contained and can be shared as is. The build is four short scripts, available from the UC San Diego Science Project on request: a download script that fetches every source file listed under Data and Sources, and three Python scripts that assemble the dataset, fit the models, and regenerate this page. CAST results are released each October alongside the California School Dashboard, so the refresh is an annual, roughly one-hour task. The same scripts work for any California county by changing the county codes, which is how another California Science Project site could reproduce this for its own region.

    Data and Sources

    • CAST research files (all years): CAASPP Research Files for California Science Test. Statewide "All Student Groups" caret-delimited files: cast_ca2019_all_csv_v1, cast_ca2021_all_csv_v2, cast_ca2022_all_csv_v1, cast_ca2023_all_csv_v1, cast_ca2024_all_csv_v1, cast_ca2025_all_csv_v1, cast_ca2026_all_csv_v1; plus the Tests and StudentGroups lookup tables and the annual entities files.
    • Research file layouts: 2025-26 CAST Research File Layout (earlier years linked from the same page).
    • Dashboard Census Enrollment data files (2019 through 2026): CDE Dashboard Enrollment Downloadable Data Files; record layout at CDE.
    • Free or Reduced-Price Meal (Student Poverty) data, 2018-19 through 2025-26: CDE Unduplicated Student Poverty files.
    • Public Schools and Districts directory: CDE Public Schools and Districts Data Files (tab-delimited export, retrieved October 18, 2026).
    • Method background: the "beating the odds" residual approach follows the school-effectiveness tradition (for example, the Educational Opportunity Project at Stanford, Reardon and colleagues) and the California School Dashboard's own similar-schools logic. These are mainstream, established methods in the field.
    • Companion dashboard: San Diego and Imperial Counties: K-12 Science Professional Learning and Curriculum Landscape (an audit of district LCAPs and science staffing), v1.3, October 2026, UC San Diego Science Project. Available on request.
